His words "with insight" — Ibn al-A'rabi said: "Insight is steadfastness in religion." It was also said: "Insight is lesson (ibrah)," as one says, "Do you not have insight (basirah) in such a matter?" meaning a lesson. The poet said:
"Among the former generations who have passed, for us there are insights (basa'ir)."
The verified view: lesson is the fruit of insight; when one sees clearly he takes lesson, and whoever lacks lesson is as if he had no insight.
The root of the word is manifestation and clarity, so the Qur'an is "insights" (basa'ir), meaning evidences, guidance, and clarification that lead to the truth and guide to right conduct.
For this reason the trace of blood by which one tracks a shot animal is called "basirah."
The verse also indicates that whoever is not upon insight is not a follower of the Messenger, and that his followers are people of insight. For this reason He said: "I and whoever follows me." If the meaning is "I invite to Allah, I and whoever follows me," with "whoever follows me" conjoined to the pronoun in "I invite," the conjunction is admissible because of the separating phrase, and it is an indication that the followers of the Messenger are those who call to Allah and to His Messenger. If it is conjoined to the pronoun in "my way," meaning "this is my way and the way of whoever follows me," the same holds. In both cases, his way and the way of his followers is the call to Allah.
The fourth principle is His words: ﴿guiding by Our command﴾. This indicates their following what Allah revealed to His Messenger, and their guidance by it alone, not by other sayings, opinions, sects, or doctrines. Indeed they guide only by His command specifically.
From this it results that the leaders of religion whom people follow are those who combined patience and certainty and the call to Allah through the Sunnah and revelation, not through opinions and innovations. These are the successors of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his community; they are his elite and his allies. Whoever opposes or fights them has opposed Allah, glory be to Him, and has given Him notice of war.
Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said in the introduction of his book refuting the Jahmiyyah: "Praise be to Allah who placed in every period, in the interval between messengers, remnants of people of knowledge who call those who have gone astray to guidance, and who endure harm from them. They give life to the dead through the Book of Allah, and give sight to the blind through the light of Allah. How many a slain one of Iblis have they revived, and how many a lost wanderer have they guided! How good is their effect upon people, and how evil is the effect of people upon them! They refute from the Book of Allah the distortion of extremists, the false claims of falsifiers, and the interpretation of the ignorant, who have raised the banners of innovation and let loose the reins of strife. They dispute about the Book, oppose the Book, and unite on abandoning the Book; they speak about Allah, concerning Allah, and concerning the Book of Allah without knowledge; they speak with the ambiguous parts of speech and deceive the ignorant people with what resembles truth for them. So we seek refuge in Allah from the trials of misleaders."

(Section)
Among what deserves attention in knowledge, recognition, intention, and will is the knowledge that every person, indeed every living creature, strives for what brings him pleasure, bliss, and a good life, and by which the opposites of that are repelled. This is a sound objective that comprises six matters:
The first is knowing the thing that is beneficial to the servant, suitable to him, whose attainment brings his pleasure, joy, happiness, and good life.
The second is knowing the path that leads to it.
The third is traveling that path.
The fourth is knowing the harmful, injurious, repugnant thing that troubles his life.
The fifth is knowing the path which, if he travels it, leads him to that.
The sixth is avoiding traveling it.
These are six matters, and the servant's pleasure, happiness, joy, and the soundness of his condition are not complete except by completing them; whatever is lacking of them returns with evil to his condition and troubles his life.
Every intelligent person strives for these matters, but most people err in attaining this sought-after, beloved, beneficial objective, either by not conceiving and knowing it, or by not knowing the path that leads to it. These two errors have ignorance as their cause, and one is freed from them by knowledge.
It may happen that he has knowledge of the objective and knowledge of its path, but in his heart there are desires and appetites that come between him and the intention of this beneficial objective and the traveling of its path. Whenever he wishes to do so, those appetites and desires confront him and stand between him and it, and he cannot abandon them and prefer this objective over them except by one of two things: either an attachment of love, or a disturbing fear. Thus God and His Messenger, the Last Abode, Paradise and its bliss become more beloved to him than these appetites, and he knows he cannot combine them, so he prefers the higher of the two beloved things over the lower. Or there arises in him knowledge of what follows from preferring these appetites, of fears and pains whose pain is greater than the pain of losing these appetites and more lasting. When these two kinds of knowledge are firmly established in his heart, they produce in him the preference of what should be preferred over everything else. For the distinguishing quality of intellect is preferring the higher of two beloved things over the lower, and bearing the lesser of two hardships in order to be freed from the greater.
By this principle the intellects of people are known, the intelligent are distinguished from others, and their differences in intellect become apparent. How far is the intellect of one who prefers a fleeting, troubled, embittering pleasure, which is like a jumble of dreams or like a phantom visited in sleep, over a pleasure that is among the greatest pleasures and a joy and delight among the greatest, lasting, never passing away, never ceasing! He sold it for that fleeting, vanishing pleasure filled with pains, whose attainment came through pains and whose outcome is pains. If the intelligent person weighed its pleasure against its pain, its harm against its benefit, he would be ashamed before himself and his intellect: how could he strive to seek it and waste his time in preoccupation with it, let alone prefer it over what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived?
Allah, glory be to Him, has purchased from the believers their selves and made their price Paradise, and carried out this contract through His Messenger and intimate friend and the best of His creation. So the commodity of the Lord of the heavens and earth is its purchaser, and enjoying the gazing upon His noble face and hearing His speech from Him in His abode is its price, and the contract was executed through His Messenger. How is it fitting for an intelligent person to waste it, neglect it, and sell it for a paltry price in a passing, vanishing, perishing abode? Is this not among the greatest deceptions? This enormous deception will only become apparent to him on the Day of Mutual Deception, when the scales of the God-fearing are heavy and the scales of the falsifiers are light.

(Section: On the reports from the Companions and those after them concerning the virtue of patience)

Imam Ahmad said: We were told by Waki', from Malik ibn Mughul, from al-Safar, who said: Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, fell ill, and people visited him. They said: "Shall we call a physician for you?" He said: "The physician has already seen me." They said: "What did he say to you?" He said: "He said: 'I do what I will.'"

Imam Ahmad also said: We were told by Abu Mu'awiyah, from al-A'mash, from Mujahid, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We have found our best living through patience."

He also said: "The best life we have experienced was through patience. If patience had been a man, he would have been noble."

Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed patience in relation to faith is like the head to the body. When the head is severed, the body perishes." Then he raised his voice and said: "Indeed there is no faith for one who has no patience." And he said: "Patience is a mount that does not stumble."

Al-Hasan said: "Patience is one of the treasures of good. Allah does not bestow it except upon a noble servant of His."

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "Allah does not bestow a blessing upon a servant and then take it from him, and replace it with patience, except that what He gives in its place will be better than what He took."

Maymun ibn Mihran said: "Nothing is like patience for a person who has lost something of goodness, however small."

Sulayman ibn al-Qasim said: "Every deed has a known reward except patience. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾. He said: 'like overflowing water.'"

One of the knowers of God kept a slip of paper in his pocket that he would take out from time to time and look at, on which was written: ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, for indeed you are in Our eyes﴾.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If patience and gratitude were two camels, I would not mind which one I rode."

When Muhammad ibn Shubrumah was afflicted with a trial, he would say: "A summer cloud, and then it will clear away."

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, commenting on the verse ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient﴾, said: "When they took hold of the head of the matter, We made them heads."

It was said to al-Ahnaf ibn Qays: "What is forbearance (hilm)?" He said: "That you be patient with what you dislike, for a while."

(Qā'idah: a principle)

Seeking is the pollinating partner (liqah, lit. cross-fertilization) of faith. When seeking and faith come together, they yield righteous deeds. Good opinion of Allah is the pollinating partner of need for Him and dependence upon Him. When these two come together, they yield the answering of supplication. Fear (khashyah) is the pollinating partner of love (mahabbah). When these come together, they yield compliance with commands and avoidance of prohibitions. Patience is the pollinating partner of certainty (yaqin). When these come together, they bequeath leadership in religion. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs﴾.

The soundness of following the Messenger is the pollinating partner of sincerity. When these come together, they yield the acceptance of deeds and reliance upon them. Action is the pollinating partner of knowledge. When these come together, there is success and happiness. If either one stands alone without the other, it benefits nothing. Forbearance is the pollinating partner of knowledge. When these come together, there is mastery of this world and the next, and the knowledge of the scholar is beneficial. If either one stands apart from its companion, benefit is lost. Resolve is the pollinating partner of insight. When these come together, their possessor attains the good of this world and the next, and his aspiration reaches the highest place in every respect. Shortfalls in perfections arise either from lack of insight or from lack of resolve. Good intention is the pollinating partner of soundness of mind. If both are lacking, all good is lost, and when they come together they yield every kind of good. Soundness of judgment is the pollinating partner of courage. When these come together, there is victory and triumph. If they are absent, there is abandonment and failure. If judgment exists without courage, there is cowardice and incapacity. If courage exists without judgment, there is recklessness and ruin. Patience is the pollinating partner of insight. When these come together, the good lies in their combination. Al-Hasan said: "If you wish to see an insightful person who is not patient, you will not see one. And if you wish to see a patient person who lacks insight, you will not see one. If you see a patient person who is insightful, then that is the one." Sincere counsel is the pollinating partner of intellect. The more sincere counsel grows strong, the more the intellect grows strong and luminous. Remembrance and reflection are each the pollinating partner of the other. When they come together, they produce renunciation of this world and desire for the next. Piety is the pollinating partner of reliance upon Allah. When these come together, the heart is made upright. The pollinating partner of taking up the readiness for the encounter is the shortening of hope. When these come together, all good lies in their union, and evil lies in their separation. The pollinating partner of lofty resolve is correct intention. When these come together, the servant reaches the utmost of what is sought.
